Bath.metaTitle: Bath, ME Wildlife Removal | City of Ships, Kennebec River
Bath.metaDescription: Bats, rats, raccoons and squirrels in Bath, ME. Historic homes on Washington Street and near the shipyard and Kennebec River — same-day service, call us.
Bath.housing_era: Bath, the City of Ships, has a rich stock of large historic homes along Washington Street and the South End from its shipbuilding wealth, brick downtown blocks on Front Street, and post-war neighborhoods in the north. Big attics, multiple chimneys and old foundations are typical downtown.
Bath.geographic_features: Kennebec River (wide river along the eastern edge of the city), Bath waterfront and shipyard (working shipbuilding waterfront), Winnegance Bay area (tidal waters south of the city), Nequasset Brook drainage (stream corridors in the western neighborhoods)
neighborhoods: Downtown and Front Street (historic blocks and nearby homes)
Washington Street and South End (large historic shipbuilder homes)
North Bath (post-war and rural homes)
Centre Street area (residential streets west of downtown)
High Street area (older homes on the hill above downtown)
Bath.wildlife_intro:
Bath's grand shipbuilder homes and working waterfront shape its wildlife work. Bats are a leading call in the big Washington Street and South End houses, where large attics and old chimneys host summer colonies. Raccoons work chimneys and waterfront waste, gray squirrels fill the canopy streets, and Norway rats appear around the waterfront, shipyard-adjacent blocks and restaurant waste downtown. Skunks den under porches across the older neighborhoods, and the Kennebec River corridor keeps animals moving along the city's eastern edge all night.

Historic Bath homes need detailed exclusion: multiple chimneys, dormers and trim gaps mean a bat job here is a whole-roofline plan, and we explain it that way. Winter brings squirrel and raccoon attic calls, spring brings litters, and summer is for inspecting bat colonies and scheduling exclusions in the proper window under Maine guidance. We take care to seal in ways that suit historic masonry and woodwork, because in Bath the houses themselves are a large part of what owners are protecting.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Bath?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the house needs, so we do not quote a firm price before looking. A simple squirrel entry sealed early costs far less than a long-standing bat roost or raccoon damage in an attic. Call us for an inspection and we will explain the options and the cost in writing before any work starts, with no pressure to decide on the spot.

faqs.q: Why do Bath's big historic homes seem to get bats more than newer houses?
faqs.a: Size and age: more chimneys, more roof junctions, larger attics and a century of small gaps give bats choices a newer, tighter house does not. A colony also returns to a roost that works, so an old house can host bats for many summers. Thorough exclusion breaks that cycle by closing every gap after the bats leave through one-way devices.

Topsham.wildlife_intro:
Topsham's blend of historic village homes, Highland Green and newer subdivisions produces varied work for our crew. In the village, bats and squirrels use the older chimneys and eaves along Main Street, while raccoons and skunks work porches and trash across town. The Cathance and Androscoggin river corridors bring beavers to culverts and keep raccoons moving through the Foreside and eastern neighborhoods. Newer subdivisions see squirrels in vents and attics surprisingly quickly once street trees mature, and groundhogs work the garden edges on rural lots.

A Topsham inspection often covers two worlds in one street: a historic house needing detailed bat sealing next to a newer home needing a vent screen and a chimney cap. Winter denning drives attic calls, and spring reveals skunk dens and vole damage in lawns after snowmelt. Our crew plans each house on its own construction, seals the entries we find, and advises on the waste and feed storage that keeps raccoons from treating a neighborhood as a nightly route.

faqs.q: Beavers are damming the Cathance River near our Topsham home — what are our options?
faqs.a: Options depend on what is being flooded and Maine's rules for beaver work, and they range from protecting culverts and using flow devices to removal by an MDIFW-certified Animal Damage Control agent where that is warranted. Breaking a dam out by hand usually buys only a few nights. Call us to see the site and we will explain which option fits your property.

Phippsburg.wildlife_intro:
Phippsburg's peninsula of cottages and fishing homes gives wildlife long quiet stretches to move in. Bats roost in the attics of Popham Beach and Small Point cottages through summer, raccoons den in chimneys of homes closed for winter, and skunks live under porches and steps all along Route 209. Phippsburg Center's older village homes get squirrels and bats in the usual pattern, and the marshes of the Morse and Sprague rivers keep raccoons traveling between shore neighborhoods at night.

Spring openings and fall closings frame our Phippsburg calendar. A closing visit that caps chimneys, screens vents and seals crawl spaces prevents most winter tenancy, and an opening inspection catches the rest before families settle in. Bat work in cottages that sit unoccupied follows Maine's restriction on excluding unoccupied buildings in June and July, so timing is planned openly with owners and caretakers. We aim to complete Phippsburg jobs in coordinated trips down the peninsula, inspection to sealing.

faqs.q: Our Popham cottage is closed all winter — what is the single best prevention step?

A full fall sealing inspection is better still, since crawl spaces and eaves weather open in coastal storms. We can do the closing check and leave you a short list of anything that needs attention before next season.

Georgetown.housing_era: Georgetown is an island-like peninsula town of fishing village homes in Five Islands and Robinhood, seasonal cottages near Reid State Park, and wooded rural homes along Route 127. Many shore properties are part-year residences with older chimneys and crawl spaces.
Georgetown.geographic_features: Kennebec River (river along the western side of town), Sheepscot Bay (bay along the eastern shore), Reid State Park and Griffiths Head (state park beaches and rocky headland), Robinhood Cove and Back River (tidal coves in the northern part of town)

Georgetown.wildlife_intro:
Georgetown's fishing villages and park-side cottages produce a quieter version of the Midcoast seasonal pattern. Raccoons work the Five Islands waterfront and den in chimneys of homes in Robinhood and Georgetown Center, bats roost in cottages that sit empty near Reid State Park, and skunks den under porches along Route 127. Gray squirrels enter attics where the woods meet a roofline, which in Georgetown is nearly everywhere. Opossums show up occasionally near shore homes, usually around pet food or compost, and move on once food is secured.

With many homes part-year and the town spread along one road, our Georgetown work is planned as complete visits: inspect the attic, chimney and crawl space, clear any animals, and seal in one coordinated trip where conditions allow. Fall closing checks are the highest-value service here, because a cottage sealed in October rarely greets its owner with a raccoon in May. Bat timing follows Maine's rules for unoccupied buildings, and we will tell you plainly if a colony's exclusion needs to wait for its window.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the house needs, so we do not quote a firm price before looking. A simple squirrel entry sealed early costs far less than a long-standing bat roost or raccoon damage in an attic. faqs.q: We found a skunk under our Georgetown cottage steps — can it be moved without spraying?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, with the right approach. Skunks spray when startled or cornered, so calm trapping or a one-way exit fitted to the den, handled by our crew, greatly lowers the odds. Timing matters if young skunks are present in spring. After the den is clear we screen the opening with buried hardware cloth so the space is not reused.

Richmond.wildlife_intro:
Richmond's river village homes and inland farms give our crew a mix of town and country calls. Bats and gray squirrels are common in the older Main Street and Front Street houses, raccoons den in chimneys and barns, and skunks work porches and outbuildings from the village to the farms on Route 197. The Kennebec River and Swan Island's woods keep wildlife close to the village edge, and beavers occasionally block culverts on the Abagadasset River and smaller streams, flooding yards and camp roads.

Winter attic calls in the village and spring skunk and raccoon work on the farms set the rhythm here. Because many Richmond properties include barns and sheds that store feed or equipment, we inspect outbuildings along with the house and include them in the sealing plan where wildlife is actually using them. A farmhouse sealed tight while raccoons den in the attached barn is only half a job, and we would rather tell you that on the first visit than return for the other half later.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Richmond?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the house needs, so we do not quote a firm price before looking. A simple squirrel entry sealed early costs far less than a long-standing bat roost or raccoon damage in an attic. Call us for an inspection and we will explain the options and the cost in writing before any work starts, with no pressure to decide on the spot.

faqs.q: Are bats in a Richmond barn worth doing anything about?
faqs.a: If the barn stores feed, hay or equipment you handle often, or the colony is large and growing, yes: guano buildup and yearly growth make it better handled sooner. Exclusion works on barns the same way as houses, with one-way exits and sealing, timed for the season. If the barn is unused and the colony small, we will tell you honestly that monitoring may be the reasonable choice.

West Bath.wildlife_intro:
West Bath's wooded lots and two river frontages keep wildlife close to almost every home. Raccoons den in chimneys and barns, gray squirrels enter attics where big trees overhang roofs, and skunks settle under porches and sheds across town. Bats turn up in older farmhouses, and shore homes on the Kennebec and New Meadows rivers add seasonal properties that can host animals over winter. Groundhogs work gardens and field edges in summer, and beavers occasionally cause water trouble on the inland streams and pond outlets.

Our West Bath jobs are usually whole-property jobs: house, barn and porch den handled in one plan. Winter brings the attic and chimney calls as animals seek heated buildings, and spring brings litters and skunks. We seal entries, cap chimneys and screen the openings that matter, and we advise on feed and trash storage for the many West Bath properties that keep animals or large gardens. The aim is a property that stays quiet, not a single removal that has to be repeated next season.

A simple squirrel entry sealed early costs far less than a long-standing bat roost or raccoon damage in an attic. faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing by our West Bath garden and shed — should both spots be treated?
faqs.a: They are likely the same animal or family using one burrow system with several entrances, which is common. Removing the animals and then closing the burrow entrances with buried barriers addresses both spots at once. Filling one entrance while groundhogs are active just shifts them to the other, so an inspection to map the system comes first.

Woolwich.wildlife_intro:
Woolwich wraps around Montsweag Bay between two tidal rivers, and that water-and-woods setting keeps raccoons, skunks and squirrels in steady contact with homes. Raccoons travel the bay shoreline and den in farmhouse chimneys, bats roost in older homes near the village and Day's Ferry, and gray squirrels work the wooded lots along Route 1. Skunks den under porches across town, groundhogs use the field and garden edges, and beavers periodically flood culverts on the streams feeding the bay and Nequasset Lake.

The Woolwich pattern is seasonal in the Maine way: attics and chimneys in winter, litters and skunks in spring, and burrows and beaver water in summer. Shore homes that sit quiet in winter get spring-opening checks from our crew, while year-round farmhouses get full inspections that include barns and outbuildings. We seal what we find, cap chimneys, and handle beaver and rabies-vector work as an MDIFW-certified Animal Damage Control agent, explaining the legal options for each situation before work begins.

A simple squirrel entry sealed early costs far less than a long-standing bat roost or raccoon damage in an attic. Call us for an inspection and we will explain the options and the cost in writing before any work starts, with no pressure to decide on the spot.

faqs.q: We hear bats in the walls of our Woolwich farmhouse each summer — what is the process?
faqs.a: We start with an inspection and a dusk watch to find where bats enter, then fit one-way exits at the right season so the colony leaves on its own, and seal every gap once the house is clear. Bats in walls are never trapped or poisoned in our work. Timing follows Maine guidance to protect young bats, and we will map out the schedule for your house at the inspection.
